summary:
Same-sex relations are legal throughout Italy for men and women, and the age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, a parity that predates the twentieth century. Cross-dressing is legal. The penal code of the 1920s–1940s banned it and police targeted transgender people during that period; a police officer was reportedly dismissed in 2006 for cross-dressing in public while off duty.

Italy has no single comprehensive law covering sexual orientation and gender identity; protection rests on court rulings and sectoral statutes. Sexual-orientation discrimination in employment has been illegal nationwide since July 2003 under Legislative Decree no. 216 of 2003, which implements EU Directive 2000/78/EC; Law no. 101 of 2008 removed the exemptions that had covered police, armed forces and rescue services. No other nationwide law covers sexual orientation or gender identity, and no Italian law explicitly bans transphobic discrimination, leaving transgender people exposed to discrimination in goods and services, housing, education and health care. ILGA-Europe's 2021 review recorded the absence of nationwide protection in goods and services. A Rome court ruled on 15 January 2023 that firing a transgender professor amounted to sex discrimination.

Two legislative attempts to widen protection failed or narrowed. A broader anti-discrimination and hate-crime bill passed the Chamber of Deputies 265–193 on 4 November 2020 and died in the Senate on 27 October 2021 on a 131–154 secret ballot. A separate bill banning homophobic and transphobic advertising in streets and on vehicles passed the Chamber 271–16 on 28 October 2021 and the Senate 190–34 on 4 November 2021, was signed by President Mattarella and took effect on 10 November 2021; the government forced a single up-or-down vote on the whole text, so members who opposed that provision had to vote for it.

Nine regions have adopted their own anti-discrimination statutes: Tuscany (2004), Liguria (2009), Marche (2010), Sicily (2015), Piedmont (2016), Umbria (2017), Emilia-Romagna (2019), Campania (2020) and Apulia (2024). Coverage therefore varies by region.

Legal gender change has been available since 1982, when Italy became the sixth country in the world to permit it; since 21 May 2015 neither sterilisation nor sex reassignment surgery has been required. On 23 July 2024 the Constitutional Court, in judgment no. 143, recognised non-binary people as rights-holders under Articles 2, 3 and 32 of the Constitution but declined to create a non-binary registry marker, holding that only Parliament can alter the male/female binary; the same judgment struck down the requirement of judicial authorisation for gender-affirming surgery after a legal sex change. Courts in Trento (15 February 2023) permitted legal gender change for transgender minors with parental consent and psychological consultation, and in Trapani (6 July 2023) allowed a name and gender change without surgery or hormones.

On 14 April 2025 the Court of Cassation ordered Italian identity cards to use the gender-neutral term "genitori" rather than "mother" and "father" for children with same-sex parents, finding the earlier wording discriminatory.

Partner recognition is partial. Marriages between people of the same legal sex performed abroad are registered as civil unions rather than marriages (Court of Cassation, May 2018). Citing the Constitutional Court's 2010 ruling that recognised same-sex couples as a "legitimate social formation", the Court of Cassation ordered a questura to grant a residence permit to an Algerian citizen married to a same-sex Spanish spouse. Persecution based on sexual orientation or gender identity is recognised as grounds for asylum under the 1951 Geneva Convention and EU Qualification Directive 2011/95/EU; Decree-Law No. 130/2020, in force from 22 October 2020, simplified asylum procedures and reinforced protection for vulnerable groups including people persecuted on those grounds.

Health care access is comparatively broad. Since February 2019 puberty blockers and cross-sex hormones have been provided free of charge under the National Health Service, and since 2020 hormone therapy has been fully covered. In 2018 the Italian National Bioethics Committee and the Italian Medicines Agency backed puberty blockers for adolescents with gender dysphoria case by case with safeguards; access still requires medical evaluation, parental consent and the exhaustion of other interventions, a position supported by the Italian Society of Endocrinology, the Italian Academy of Pediatrics and six other paediatric and adolescent medical societies. Gay and bisexual men have been allowed to donate blood since 2001.

Violence against transgender people is documented, and some cases have produced convictions. On 5 July 2024 a Milan traffic officer was sentenced to 10 months for beating a transgender woman with a baton. Convictions for the assault of transgender tourists were upheld on appeal (ANSA, Campania, April 2026). ILGA-Europe's 2026 review, covering 2025, records continuing homophobic and transphobic violence, including organised dating-app entrapment schemes targeting gay men. In March the Civil Court of Asti recognised for the first time physical and psychological harm caused by homophobic mistreatment. Progetto Gionata describes transphobia as the most severe and widespread discrimination facing transgender people in Italy.

Official and political signals are mixed. ILGA-Europe's 2026 review records that the Education Ministry omitted LGBTI persecution from its Holocaust Remembrance Day circulars for a second year. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 states that political rhetoric hostile to LGBT people contributes to a hostile environment in Italy.
tangentialFactors:
A cardinal publicly described homosexual acts as a mortal sin, a statement from the Catholic hierarchy rather than from the state.

In May 2026 AGESCI, Italy's largest Catholic scout association, decided after three years of internal debate that sexual orientation and gender identity can no longer exclude adults from leadership and educational roles.

Pew found in 2013 that 86% of Italians aged 18–29 accepted homosexuality, against 67% of those over 50, a generational gap that predates the current legal debate.
localsOnly:
The Ludwig Boltzmann Institute's national report of July 2025 examines LGBTIQ detainees in Italian detention, covering homolesbobitransphobia and discrimination, pathways to gender affirmation, same-sex relationships and the legal and policy framework that applies to LGBTIQ people in custody.

A 2026 thematic analysis in Frontiers in Psychiatry of transgender identity and psychiatric care in Italian prisons identifies systemic gaps and institutional challenges for incarcerated transgender people.

The Constitutional Court's July 2024 judgment left the creation of a non-binary registry marker to Parliament; no legislation on that point is sourced.

Enforcement data on hate-crime prosecutions and on the regional anti-discrimination statutes is not sourced, so the practical effect of the regional patchwork is unresolved.
